title: Cognitive Evolutionary Search to Select Feature Interactions for Click-Through Rate Prediction

problem.claim: Click-through rate prediction depends importantly on selecting feature interactions.

gap.claim: Most existing approaches use the same pre-defined interaction operation under expert guidance, which can introduce noise through improper interactions and complicate training.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes a Cognitive EvoLutionary Search framework that adaptively selects operations for interacting feature pairs under task guidance.

The framework models interactions as genomes, models as organisms, and tasks as natural environments, using model fitness to plan and visualize an evolution path for interaction modeling and selection.
The framework includes individual-based and population-based search instantiations that produce diverse models for different tasks and data.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that individual mutation and population crossover enable the framework to evolve diverse models suitable for various tasks and data.
The authors report extensive experiments on real-world datasets.
The authors report that the framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

narrative_sequence.summary: Feature-interaction selection is important for click-through rate prediction in intelligent marketing systems.
Existing approaches commonly rely on one pre-defined interaction operation and expert guidance, risking noisy or unnecessarily complex training.
The authors introduce a task-guided evolutionary framework that adaptively selects interaction operations and represents the process through an organism-environment analogy.
The framework is instantiated through individual-based and population-based search, including mutation and crossover mechanisms.
Experiments on real-world datasets are reported to show significant improvement over state-of-the-art approaches.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, or numerical effect sizes.
The abstract does not describe the selected interaction operations or the search and training costs.
The abstract does not provide implementation details sufficient to assess reproducibility.
